chunks: Parasitic R, L, C and Z0. The question: Describe the parasitic R, L, and C components that impact characteristic impedance.
"Parasitic" means a small unwanted effect that comes along with every real wire. Every trace has resistance, inductance and capacitance spread along its length.
The inductance and capacitance per meter decide its characteristic impedance, the resistance it looks like to a fast signal. The resistance just wastes a little energy.
Vias and pads add small extra bits of inductance or capacitance at single spots, and those spots can bounce part of a fast edge back.
Picture a signal as a wave moving down a canal. A side pool beside the canal soaks up some water as the wave passes, so the wave briefly weakens: that is extra capacitance.
A narrow stretch resists the flow and pushes back: that is extra inductance. A slow swell barely notices either. A sharp wave feels both.
A via or connector reduces to a series inductance plus a shunt capacitance in the middle of otherwise uniform line. The inductor lifts the local impedance, the capacitor drops it.
Parasitic: a small unwanted resistance, inductance or capacitance that comes with a real part or wire.
Per-meter inductance and capacitance ( L' , C' ): how much of each one meter of line has ("Real TL distributed RLGC model").
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance the line looks like to a traveling signal, square root of L' over C' ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Via: a plated hole joining two board layers. It adds a little inductance. Pad: the copper patch a part is soldered to. It adds a little capacitance.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from low to high, often in picoseconds (ps, trillionths of a second).
A coax cable (a center wire inside a round shield) has 250 nanohenries of inductance and 100 picofarads of capacitance per meter.
Then Z 0 equals square root of 250 nanohenries over 100 picofarads equals 50 ohms. Now add a 0. 5 picofarads pad.
It dips the local impedance and reflects about 12% of a 100 picoseconds edge. A slow 500 picoseconds edge reflects only about 2. 5%.
The same pad is harmless at low speed and a problem at high speed. That is the whole idea.
"Per unit length, L' is the magnetic energy of the trace-plus-return loop, C' is the electric energy between trace and plane, and together they set Z 0 equals square root of L' over C' .
R' and G' add loss and only matter for Z 0 at low frequency.

On a real board the bigger problem is lumped parasitics from vias, pads and connectors: a shunt capacitance dips the impedance, a series inductance bumps it, and the size of the reflection depends on how that parasitic compares with the edge rate."
